parole.significato: equivalent of English -th, -eth; suffix for ordinal numbers
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *-dô, cognate with English -th. The -n- is generalized from those stems that ended in -n originally, e.g. ti-ende from *tehun-dô.
From Old Danish bar, Old West Norse berr (with ʀ-umlaut), from Proto-Germanic *bazaz.
From Proto-Germanic *blisk (“to burn, shine”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to shine”).

From Old Danish bræd, from Proto-Germanic *brezdaz, cognate with Norwegian bredd, Swedish brädd, Old English breord. Related to *bruzdaz (“thorn”) (Danish brod) and possibly also *burdą (“board”) (Danish bord).
From Old Danish brøtæ, possibly from Proto-Germanic *brautiją, derived from *breutaną (“to break”) (Danish bryde).
From Proto-Germanic *bulljō, from Proto-Indo-European *bhljā (“testicle”), probably because of the similarity of the berry to testicles.

From Old Danish etærkop, ederkoppæ; ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aitrą (“poison”) + *kuppaz (“something round”). Identical in formation to English attercop and Old Swedish eterkoppe (whence dialectal Swedish etterkoppa).
From Old Danish ænkia (“widow”), from Old Norse (east) *enkja, (west) ekkja, from Proto-Germanic *ainakjǭ, cognate with Swedish änka.
From Old Danish fiart, from Proto-Germanic *fertaną, from Proto-Indo-European *perd-. Cognate with Old Norse fretr and Greek πορδή (pordí).

parole.significato: lint, a small quantity of some airy material
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *fnukaz, cognate with Swedish fnåk, Swedish fnugg, Swedish fnagg, Norwegian fnokk, and Icelandic fnykur. The ultimate origin is obscure, but perhaps an expressive or imitative formation. Compare also English fluff.
Inherited from Old Danish for, from Proto-Germanic *furai (in Western Old Norse replaced by the variant Old Norse fyrr, from Proto-Germanic *furiz, *furi, = Danish before).
From Old Danish fædherne, from the noun fæþrini, Old Norse faðerni (“paternal side”), derived from Proto-Germanic *fadrīnaz (“paternal”).

parole.significato: hold, foothold (a firm grip or stand)
parole.testo: From Old Danish fæstæ, from Proto-Germanic *fastiją, cognate with Norwegian feste, Swedish fäste. Derived from *fastuz (“firm”).
From Old Danish hielth, possibly derived from Proto-Germanic *heltą (“hilt”).

Originally, the dative of archaic hvo, from Old Danish hwa, hwo, oblique hwem, genitive hwes. In Old West Norse, the nominative and accusative of this pronoun has been replaced by another pronoun, hverr, but the dative and genitive are still extant: hveim, hves. From Proto-Germanic *hwaz (“who”), co
From Proto-Germanic *wepsō-, from Proto-Indo-European *wobʰseh₂ (“wasp”), from *webʰ- (“weave”). Compare Norwegian Bokmål veps, Norwegian Nynorsk kvefs, Latin vespa.
From Proto-Germanic *hulþijǭ, cognate with Swedish hylla. Related to *helþaz (“frame”) (Danish hjald).

From Old Danish keed, possibly from Proto-Germanic *kaibaz (“crooked”), cf. Norwegian Nynorsk keiv (“wry, wrong, left”), keive (“left hand”), German Low German keef (“tired”). The adjective has forms with -w in Danish dialects of Jutland and Bornholm. Possibly the standard form kēð arose in the synt
Inherited from Old Danish kuldær, kul, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kulþa, *kulþō, variants of *kelþaz (“fetus”). See Swedish kull, Norwegian Bokmål kull.

A merger of two Old Norse nouns: 1. leið (“road, direction”), from Proto-Germanic *laidō, cognate with English load, lode, German Leite (“slope”), Dutch lei (“slate”). 2. hlið f (“side”), from Proto-Germanic *hliþō, cognate with Old English hliþ n.
From Proto-Germanic *luppǭ (“flea, sandflea”, originally “jumper”), from Proto-Germanic *luppijaną (“to jump, dart”) (see *hlaupaną (“to leap, jump”)).
Ultimately from the root of lys (“light, bright”) (Proto-Germanic *leuhsaz).
From Old Danish muldwarp, from Proto-Germanic *muldawurpiz, a compound of *muldō (“dirt, soil”) + *werpaną (“to throw”). Cognate with Swedish mullvad, English mouldwarp, and German Maulwurf.

From the noun Proto-Germanic *hnukkaz, *hnukkô (“hook”), cognate with Icelandic hnokki (“hook”), Old English hnocc (“hook, penis”). In the maritime meaning, it is in borrowed from Dutch nok or Low German Nock.
From Old Danish nor, from Proto-Germanic *narwaz. Related to narv and English narrow.

parole.significato: usually the same as over- in English.
parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *ubar- (“over-”). Cognate with Dutch over-, German über-, English over-, Swedish över-. More at over.

Originally a plural of penning (“coin”), related to English penny. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *panningaz. Compare Icelandic peningar, Faroese pengar, Norwegian Nynorsk pengar, Norwegian Bokmål penger, and Swedish pengar.
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *pikkaz, cognate with Norwegian pikk, Swedish pick, Dutch pik. The word is a variant of Proto-Germanic *pīkaz, which is the source of Danish pig, English pike.

From Old Danish puthæ, from Proto-Germanic *pūto (“swollen”) (compare English eelpout, Dutch puit, Low German puddig (“inflated”)), from Proto-Germanic *bu- (“to swell”). See also Norwegian pute (“pillow, cushion”), Swedish dial. puta (“to be puffed out”).
From Proto-Germanic *skalō, cognate with German Schale.

From Old Danish skul, from Proto-Germanic *skuflō, *skūblō, cognate with Swedish skovel, English shovel, German Schaufel. The Danish word is probably partially a loan from Middle Low German schuffele.
Inherited from Old Danish skurf, from Proto-Germanic *skurf-, probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Cognate of English scurf, German Schorf and Swedish skorv.

parole.significato: to blame, or rebuke someone, usually in violent, angry terms
parole.testo: From Old Danish skiældæ, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skeldaną. Equivelant to Swedish skälla (past indicative: skällde). Related to Old Norse skjalla, skella (“to slap, scold”), skald (“poet”), but also Old Frisian skelda → Saterland Frisian: skeelde; Old Saxon: *skeldan (attested in skeldāri) →
From Old Danish smælta, from Proto-Germanic *smeltaną (“to melt”).
From Old Danish spiut, from Proto-Germanic *speutą. Compare Old Norse spjót.
From Proto-Germanic *strangijaz (“tight, tense”), cf. German streng. It is variant of the adjective Proto-Germanic *strangaz, Old Norse strangr, English strong.

parole.significato: sweat (fluid that exits the body through pores)
parole.testo: From Old Danish swet, from Proto-Germanic *swaitaz, cognate with Swedish svett, Dutch zweet, German Schweiß, English sweat. A different derivation in Western Old Norse sveiti, Norwegian Bokmål svette and Norwegian Nynorsk sveitte from *swaitô.
From sauma (“to sew”), either a new formation from the noun saumr (“seam, nails”) or from Proto-Germanic *saumōną, a variant of the previous verb.

parole.significato: southern (of localities in comparison with another locality)
parole.testo: The comparative of the adverb syd, from Old Danish syndræ, Old West Norse syðri, from Proto-Germanic *sunþrizô, a comparative of *sunþraz.
From Old Danish twinling, from or related to Old Norse tvinnr, from Proto-Germanic *twinaz.
From Proto-Germanic *þweraną (“to swirl, turn”), cognate with Norwegian tvære, Swedish tvära (dialect), Old English þweran, German zweren (Bavarian).
From Old Danish thystær, from Proto-Germanic *þusiþaz. It may have been reintroduced from Norwegian Bokmål tyst and Swedish tyst in the 19th century.

From Old Danish thyrst, thørst, from Proto-Germanic *þurstuz, *þurstiz, cognate with Swedish törst, English thirst, German Durst. In Old West Norse, þyrstr is an adjective, and þorsti is used instead.
From Old Danish ullæn, from Proto-Germanic *wullīnaz, cognate with Swedish ylle, English woolen, German wollen. Derived from *wullō (“wool”).
From Old Danish wreth, Old West Norse reiðr (“angry”), from Proto-Germanic *wraiþaz. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk vreid, Swedish vred, English wroth, Dutch wreed.

From Old Danish wra, Old West Norse rá f, from Proto-Germanic *wranhō (“something crooked”), cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk ro and Swedish vrå. From Proto-Indo-European *wrónkeh₂, cognate with Latvian ròka (“arm, hand”), Lithuanian rankà, Russian рука́ (ruká) and possibly also, via Gaulish, French b

From Old Norse banna, derived from the noun bann from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“to order, ban”), cognate with Swedish banna, English ban, German bannen. Alternatively, the Scandinavian verbs are derived from the noun bann / band), which may be an early loan from Old Saxon ban.
From Old Danish byggiæ, from Old Norse byggva, byggja, from Proto-Germanic *būwijaną (or possibly *buwwēną), cognate with Swedish bygga.

parole.significato: flaske sig – work out, pan out
parole.testo: From German Low German flasken, from Middle Low German vlaschen, of obscure origin: * possibly from a regional verb built from an older root meaning "flat" (compare Proto-Germanic *flataz): with a verb-forming suffix -sk- or -k-. According to this view, a prehistoric form *flat-ka could have yielded

Either revived or borrowed from Old Norse forn or Swedish forn respectively. from Proto-Germanic *fernaz (“foregoing, previous; recent”), from Proto-Indo-European *perǝm-, *perǝ- (“fore, first”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“forth, over, across, through”). A inherited version from Old Danish for

From Old Danish hwærkin, hwærki, from Old Norse hvárki, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk korkje, Swedish varken. The neuter of the Old Norse pronoun hvár(r)gi (“either, neither”), from hvárr (“which (of two)”) + -gi (“no”). The first part goes back to Proto-Germanic *hwaþeraz (“which (of two)”), cogna
Either the old word for "copper" or some derivation from it: Old Norse eir, from Proto-Germanic *aiz.
From Old Danish kiffue, from Old Norse kífa, either a cognate of or borrowed from Middle Low German kīven, Proto-Germanic *kībaną. Other cognates are German keifen and Dutch kijven.

Maybe a euphemistic refashioning of pokker, from Middle Low German pocke, from Proto-Germanic *pukkaz, *pukkǭ (“pock; swelling”), cognate with English pock, pox, German Pocke. Alternatively from kopper, the plural of kop (“cup”) (from the cups used for blood-letting).
From Old Norse krubba, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ. Alternatively, from Middle Low German krübbe, krubbe, from Old Saxon kribbia, from Proto-West Germanic *kribbjā, from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ.
From late Old Norse lak, lakan, either from Middle Low German laken or directly from Old Saxon lakan, from Proto-Germanic *lakaną (“sheet, cloth”).

Either inherited from Old Norse *hlina or borrowed from Middle Low German lēnen, from Proto-Germanic *hlināną (“to lean”), cognate with English lean and German lehnen. In all these languages, the verb has merged with the causative *hlainijaną (“to cause to lean”). The verbs go back to

parole.significato: member of the suborder Nematocera (which includes mosquitos, midges, gnats and others)
parole.testo: From Old Danish and Old Norse myg, either borrowed from Middle Low German mügge, from Old Saxon mugga, from Proto-West Germanic *muggjā, from Proto-Germanic *mugjǭ (“midge, small fly”); or, from Proto-Germanic *mują (“small fly”). See also with Norwegian, Swedish mygg, English midge, German Mücke. T

From mange + -de, either a new formation or inherited from Old Norse *mengd, from Proto-Germanic *managiþō, cognate with Swedish mängd, Dutch menigte, Old English menigdu. Old Icelandic has a different derivation, mengi, from *managį̄, cf. English many (the noun), German Menge and Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌽𐌰𐌲𐌴𐌹 (ma

From Old Danish nokut (also nokot, nokæt, noghet), neuter form of nokær, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk noko and Swedish något. Grammaticalization of the phrase Proto-Germanic *ne wait ek hwat (or alternatively formed by analogy as a neuter to nokær within early Old Norse). See more at nogen.

From Old Danish nār, which may derive from Proto-Germanic *nēhwōz, an alternative form of Danish nær (“nearer”), from Old Norse nær, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwiz. In Swedish, the conjunction has the form när. Alternatively, it is an abbreviation of the interrogative adverb hvornår. In earlier Danish

From Old Danish nykil, cognate with Swedish nyckel and Norwegian nøkkel, possibly identical to the following word. Alternatively, it is a younger form, with dissimilation, of Old Danish lykil (cf. also Jutlandic løgel), from Old Norse lykill, derived from the verb lúka (“to close, lock”), from Proto

Continuing Old Danish rath, from Old Norse ráð n, from Proto-Norse *ᚱᚨᛞᚨ n (*rada), either from *ᚱᚨᛞᚨᛉ m (*radaʀ) or from Proto-Germanic *rēdą n, from *rēdaz m. Cognate with Old English rǣd m (whence archaic English rede), Middle Low German rât (whence German Low German Raad), and Old High German rā

parole.significato: foam, froth (a mass of small bubbles in a liquid)
parole.testo: Either from an unattested Old Norse *skúm or borrowed from Middle Low German schūm, from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz m (“foam”), cognate with German Schaum, Dutch schuim, English scum.

From Old Danish staa, either from an unattested Eastern Old Norse *stá or borrowed from Middle Low German stān. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stāną. C.f. also stande. Cognate with German stehen, Dutch staan. Compare also Swedish stå, Norwegian Bokmål stå, English stand, Latin stāre, stō.

Possibly from (obsolete) størres (“to increase”) + -else (“act of”). The verb goes back to Old Norse stœra (“to make bigger”), from Proto-Germanic *stōrijaną, derived from *stōraz (“big, strong”). Alternatively, the Danish noun is derived directly from the adjective stor, compare tykkelse.

From Old Norse svar (“answer, reply”), either derived from the verb svara or inherited from Proto-Germanic *swarō (“solemn statement”), cognate with English swear (compare sværge (“swear”), from Proto-Germanic *swarjaną). Compare also the compound *andaswarō (“reply”) in English answer and Danish an

From Old Danish tro, late Old Norse trú, either a native derivation from the verb or borrowed from Middle Low German trouwe, trūwe, from Proto-Germanic *trewwō (“fidelity, pledge”), cognate with English truce, German Treue (“loyalty”).

From Middle High German or Middle Low German tūten. The verb is either an independent onomatopoeic formation or derived, with an irregular treatment of the initial consonant, from Proto-Germanic *þeutaną (“to howl”), which is the source of Old Norse þjóta, Swedish tjuta, Old English þēotan, Old High
From Old Norse vǫllr, from Proto-Germanic *walþuz (“forest”), cognate with German Wald. Doublet of vold. Alternatively, the same word as the noun above.
From Old Danish warm, from Old Norse varmr, from Proto-Germanic *warmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”) or alternatively *wer- (“to burn”).
From Old Danish wiskæ, either borrowed from Middle Low German wischen or inherited directly from Proto-Germanic *wiskijaną, cognate with German wischen.
